title: How Automats Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the automat, the self-service cafeteria chain with glass-fronted coin-operated food compartments. They trace its origin in Berlin in 1895, its arrival in the U.S. through Joseph Horn and Frank Hardart in Philadelphia (1902) and New York (1912), its famous nickel coffee and pie, its treatment of customers regardless of gender, race or class, its labor disputes, its decline from the 1960s due to suburbanization and changing clientele, the closing of the last New York automat in 1991, and later automat-style imitations. The episode opens with banter about Josh's illness and a new writer, Laura Claus, and ends with listener mail correcting a "Modgepodge" pronunciation.

segments.title: Opening banter and new writer
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Josh's recent trip to Mexico City and illness, the tight deadline, Chuck's antenna TV setup, and welcoming new writer Laura Claus.

segments.title: What the automat was
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the automat as a self-serve cafeteria with glass-fronted compartments opened by coin slots. They note its appeal to people who could not read, and that it was seen as high tech in the early twentieth century.

segments.title: Origins in Germany and arrival in the U.S.
segments.summary: The first automat opened in Berlin in 1895 and won a gold medal at the Brussels World Fair. Joseph Horn and Frank Hardart brought the concept to Philadelphia, where their first automat opened in 1902 after shipping and warehouse fire setbacks.

segments.title: Expansion in New York and why it succeeded there
segments.summary: Horn and Hardart entered New York in 1912 after Harcomb went out of business. By 1932 they had 42 New York automats and 20 in Philadelphia, becoming the largest U.S. restaurant chain, and they thrived during the Great Depression. Nicholas Brammel's explanation for New York's success is that restaurants clustered around dense office and shopping districts. Chuck argues that Detroit's Automatic Lunch Room Number One name hurt it.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with banter about Josh's illness.

segments.title: Cleanliness, inclusivity and the atmosphere
segments.summary: The automats were known for being clean and safe, welcoming unaccompanied women, families, and people of all classes. Their Art Deco design featured marble, stained glass and bronze. Customers could linger over a nickel coffee without staff hustling them.

segments.title: Fresh food, day-old shops and nickel coffee
segments.summary: Food was prepared fresh and unsold food was sold the next day at discount in three day-old shops in lower income New York neighborhoods. Coffee was French drip, replaced every 20 minutes and sold for a nickel, which was unusual compared to boiled, gritty coffee of the time.

segments.title: Nickel price, coin economics and nickel throwers
segments.summary: Horn and Hardart kept the nickel coffee price for 38 years, losing money, and then doubled it to a dime because the slots only took nickels. Sales dropped from 70 million to 45 million cups, but revenue stayed on top. Pie sales at breakfast are discussed, and nickel throwers, women who made change, are described.

segments.title: Pie for breakfast and Neil Simon quote
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea of eating pie for breakfast and how an automat let people do so discreetly. Neil Simon's recollection of childhood automat visits is quoted, and the hosts comment on the nostalgia.

segments.title: Food quality, the facade and labor disputes
segments.summary: Food quality likely declined toward the end. The automat was a facade: food was prepared in central commissaries and loaded into rotating drums by workers. Horn and Hardart workers struck in 1937 and 1952, and Judge Melvin Barasch described conditions as straight out of the nineteenth century in 1991. The company's president's son described company picnics.

segments.title: Employee Christmas parties and personal anecdotes
segments.summary: Apache Ramos, an actor from The Warriors who later managed the Fat Boys, worked at an automat with his grandmother, and recalled holiday parties for workers' children. Josh and Chuck share childhood anecdotes.

segments.title: Break before inclusivity segment
segments.summary: A short break is taken before returning to the topic of inclusivity.

segments.title: Inclusivity, celebrity fans and famous visitors
segments.summary: Horn and Hardart's motto was to serve everybody the same way. Colin Powell recalled the automat on 42nd Street as a diverse place, and historian Lisa Keller noted it welcomed immigrants. Celebrity visitors included Audrey Hepburn, Carl Reiner and Mel Brooks.

segments.title: Decline from the 1960s and Burger King conversions
segments.summary: Automat revenues declined from the 1960s, partly due to suburbanization, malls and fewer office workers in midtown. Attempts to revive business included a Wild West room, a beer garden, roller skating waiters and live bands. Horn and Hardart later sold valuable real estate, and Burger King franchises replaced several automat sites.

segments.title: Clientele change and downward spiral
segments.summary: As the automats declined, they attracted itinerant and unhoused people, which drove away families and the middle class. Falling business also made the central commissary model inefficient. The hosts compare the automat to fast food.

segments.title: Last New York automat and pop culture references
segments.summary: The last New York automat opened in 1977 at 200 East 42nd Street and closed in 1991, later becoming a Gap. The automat appeared in films and cartoons, including Bugs Bunny and The Flintstones, and in Russell Hoban's or Frankweiler-style children's book referenced as E. L. Konigsburg's Mixed-Up Files.
topics: Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler

segments.title: Automat revivals and imitations
segments.summary: Pat Boone's Dino Matt, Andy Warhol's planned Andy Matt, Japanese conveyor sushi, Brooklyn Dumpling Shop cubbies, and made-to-order pizza vending machines are discussed as automat-like concepts.

segments.title: Closing banter
segments.summary: Josh reports feeling better and Chuck jokes about the effect he has on Josh before moving to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Modgepodge correction
segments.summary: Listener Kelly corrects the pronunciation of Mod Podge, a craft glue, which the hosts had described as a jumble of things that do not go together. Martha Stewart confirmed she has Mod Podge.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite listener corrections by email and close with the show credit.
